items.d: Spying abroad is done under the President's power, not under a law passed by Congress. The surveillance bill changes federal criminal law. It does not mention Executive Order 12333.

inq.open: The legal references for these powers are listed so readers can check them. But the laws themselves were not opened for this review. The 2022 figures are the newest that were checked.

two.dec: Is the surveillance bill meant to change how spy agencies collect data, or only how police do?

views.why: Intelligence and counterterrorism officials would like the bill to stay silent on their powers. That silence leaves their current powers in place.
Some members of Congress want to renew current surveillance law first. They would take up wider changes later.
A coalition of privacy and civil liberties groups wants agencies to get a warrant before they search spy data. It also wants to end government buying of data from brokers without a warrant.

findings.pat: The party judges its own compliance
findings.title: Each agency would decide if collecting data needs a warrant. No one checks when the agency says no.
findings.plain: The bill would require a warrant, meaning permission from a judge, before the government searches a person's data. But the agency that wants the data would decide first if its own action counts as a search. It would also decide if one of the bill's exceptions applies, such as consent or an emergency. A judge would look at the matter only if the agency decided it needed a warrant. The bill requires no report or check when the agency decides it does not.
findings.tech: The warrant rule gives an outside check for searches that reach a judge. But the agency doing the investigating decides if a case ever reaches a judge. That agency gains from reading the word "search" narrowly and the bill's exceptions broadly. A person can sue only after learning about the search. The bill does not require anyone to tell them.
findings.use: An agency could decide that collecting someone's data needs no warrant under the surveillance bill. No judge, watchdog or member of the public would be told.

am.label: Yearly check of decisions not to seek a warrant
am.instr: Section 3119 of title 18, United States Code, as added by section 2 of this Act, is amended by adding at the end the following new subsection: "Audit.--The Inspector General of each agency that acquires data in reliance on an exception in subsection (b) shall audit a sample of those acquisitions each year and shall submit a report on the results to Congress, with a public summary.".

ops.w: Audit.--The Inspector General of each agency that acquires data in reliance on an exception in subsection (b) shall audit a sample of those acquisitions each year and shall submit a report on the results to Congress, with a public summary.

am.cost: This change would have each agency's Inspector General, its inside watchdog, check a sample of cases. These are cases where the agency collected data without a warrant. The checks would cost money. The public summary would need care so it does not reveal how investigations work. The President's branch of government picks these watchdogs. So their checks are less independent than a judge's review.

findings.title: The bill does not say when it would start or what happens to personal data agencies already hold.
findings.plain: The bill does not say when it would take effect. It also does not say what happens to data agencies already have.
findings.tech: With no start date, the bill would take effect as soon as it became law. It says nothing about keeping, deleting or still searching data gathered earlier. It also says nothing about investigations already under way.
findings.use: Agencies could keep using the sets of personal data they already hold.

findings.title: The bill does not require any reports or audits to show if agencies follow its new warrant rule.
findings.plain: The bill has no reporting rule and no audit, which is a formal check. It gives no role to an inspector general, the official who reviews an agency from inside. So there would be no regular way to know if agencies had stopped searching without warrants.
findings.tech: Surveillance laws often require yearly reports on court orders sought and granted. They also often require regular reviews by inspectors general. The right to sue depends on people learning they were searched. The bill does not require telling them.
findings.use: People could not challenge searches that break the bill's warrant rule if no one ever tells them about those searches.

findings.title: A sponsor says the bill stops federal pressure on local police to share data. The bill has no such rule.
findings.plain: One sponsor's press release says the bill would stop federal agencies from pushing local police to share surveillance data. No such rule appears in the bill as first filed.
findings.tech: The press release lists a ban on federal pressure on local police. The ban would cover data collected without a warrant. The bill says nothing about sharing data between governments or about rules tied to grants. It says nothing about fusion centers, which are shared federal and local intelligence offices. The ban may have been in an earlier draft.
findings.use: People who read the press release could think the bill already deals with federal pressure on local police. But the bill has no rule on sharing data.

findings.title: The bill limits government access to data from companies that sell personal data. It does not stop the sales.
findings.plain: The bill tells the government not to get data from data brokers without a warrant. Data brokers are companies that sell personal data. A warrant is permission from a judge. The bill does not stop those companies from collecting or selling the data. The data would still exist. So any weak spot in the rule for government would leave the data open to it.
findings.tech: Past cases show why this matters. A Defense Intelligence Agency memo, made public in 2021, described buying location data from companies. A 2022 report, once secret and now public, described spy agencies buying data from companies on a large scale. In 2025 Montana barred its own agencies from buying such data. In 2024 the House passed a bill aimed at government purchases from brokers. Neither ends the collection itself.
findings.use: Any agency or partner the bill does not reach could still buy the data from data brokers.

s.l: DIA memo on buying location data
Declassified report on commercially available information
Montana closes the data broker loophole

am.label: Broader option: limit what data brokers may sell to governments
am.instr: Add at the end of the bill the following new section: "SEC. __. PROHIBITION ON PROVIDING COVERED DATA TO GOVERNMENT ENTITIES. (a) No data broker may sell, license, or otherwise provide data described in section 3119(d)(1)(C) of title 18, United States Code, to any Federal, State, local, or foreign government entity, or to any person acting on behalf of such an entity, except as required by a warrant. (b) A violation of this section shall be treated as an unfair or deceptive act or practice under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act."

ops.w:
SEC. __. PROHIBITION ON PROVIDING COVERED DATA TO GOVERNMENT ENTITIES.
(a) No data broker may sell, license, or otherwise provide data described in section 3119(d)(1)(C) of title 18, United States Code, to any Federal, State, local, or foreign government entity, or to any person acting on behalf of such an entity, except as required by a warrant.
(b) A violation of this section shall be treated as an unfair or deceptive act or practice under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act.

am.cost: This change would bar data brokers from selling personal data to any government body without a warrant. The Federal Trade Commission, which enforces rules on businesses, would enforce it. This goes beyond the bill's stated purpose. Limits on selling information face free speech challenges. The bill would need to define "data broker". And companies that collect data directly are not brokers. Banning data brokers altogether would go further. It would have larger effects on the economy and leave the same gap for companies that collect data themselves.

two.dec: Is the surveillance bill meant only to limit what personal data the government gets? Or is it meant to end the buying and selling of that data?

views.why: Data brokers and ad tech companies would prefer a rule aimed only at the government as a buyer. That would leave their business as it is.

findings.pat: Closed exception list omits settled exceptions

a.q: Except as provided in subsection (b), no search may be conducted without a warrant

findings.title: The bill lists only six warrant exceptions. It leaves out border, vehicle and inventory searches that courts allow today.
findings.plain: The bill says no search may happen without a warrant except in six listed situations. Searches at the border, searches of cars and searches of property taken into police custody are not on the list. A court could read the list as complete, which would mean those searches need a warrant. Or a court could stretch another part of the bill to save them.
findings.tech: The bill says "no search may be conducted without a warrant" except for the six listed exceptions. That makes the list the only source of exceptions. The six are plain view, identification checks, two public information exceptions, consent and emergencies. The Supreme Court reads a list like this as closed, in United States v Johnson (2000). The Court said Congress "considered the issue of exceptions" and limited the law to the ones it listed. Border searches are a settled kind that needs no warrant. The Court explained this in United States v Flores-Montano (2004), quoting United States v Ramsey. It said such searches "are reasonable simply by virtue of the fact that they occur at the border". It also said the government's interest "is at its zenith at the international border", meaning its strongest point. The bill's definition of a search covers surveillance or questions that collect information on a person's "travel". The bill keeps constitutional protections, not government search powers. It keeps only stops, pat-downs, arrests and "searches incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". A border inspection is not clearly one of those encounters. The text does not say whether removing these exceptions is intended. A court would likely have to choose between two readings. One follows Johnson and would require warrants for these searches. The other reads the clause on ordinary law enforcement encounters broadly, which another finding in this review calls a separate risk.
findings.use: A traveler whose phone was searched at a port of entry could argue the bill required a warrant. The traveler would note that no listed exception applies. The government could say the bill or an unwritten exception keeps its border search power. The courts would decide.

findings.pat: Absolute bar collides with emergency disclosure law

a.q: without a valid warrant, regardless of whether the third party consents or cooperates

findings.title: The bill has no emergency exception for company data. Today, companies may share records when a life is in danger.
findings.plain: Today a phone or internet company may give police records at once in some emergencies. One example is a kidnapping, when someone faces death or serious injury. The bill says the government may not get a company's data without a warrant, even if the company cooperates. The bill's emergency exception is attached to a different part. So it is unclear whether this kind of sharing would still be allowed.
findings.tech: The bill bars the government from getting data held by a third party, such as a company, without a valid warrant. It says this applies "regardless of whether the third party consents or cooperates". The bill's main warrant rule begins by pointing to its list of exceptions. This rule about third parties does not. The emergency exception covers "Searched conducted under exigent circumstances", meaning urgent emergencies. That ties it to searches and not to the third party rule. Today a provider may share records if it believes "in good faith" that someone faces "danger of death or serious physical injury". The law covers communications and also other information about the emergency. These are voluntary disclosures by the provider. That is the cooperation the bill says does not replace a warrant. The bill has no clause that overrides older law. It also changes no older law to match, as another finding in this review notes. So a court would have to reconcile the two. A separate finding notes the same gap for the consent exception. This finding is about its effect on emergency access.
findings.use: A phone company could refuse an emergency request until police get a warrant. An agency could argue the older emergency law still applies.

a.q: Every person, including a Federal employee, who, under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage, of the United States

findings.title: The bill lets people sue federal officials. Settled rules would bar suits against the United States or its agencies.
findings.plain: The new right to sue covers "every person" who violates Fourth Amendment rights. The person must be acting under federal authority. Courts read "person" in a law to leave out the government unless the law clearly says otherwise, and this bill does not. So a lawsuit would name the individual officer. It would not name the agency or the United States, even if the officer followed an agency policy.
findings.tech: The bill makes "Every person, including a Federal employee" liable. It does not say "person" includes the United States or an agency. It also does not give up sovereign immunity, which is the government's protection from being sued. The Supreme Court applies a "longstanding interpretive presumption that 'person' does not include the sovereign". The Court says the presumption "may be disregarded only upon some affirmative showing" that Congress meant otherwise. The case is Return Mail Inc v United States Postal Service (2019). The Court also said, "Absent a waiver, sovereign immunity shields the Federal Government and its agencies from suit". The case is FDIC v Meyer (1994). So damages would run only against individual officers. They can be expected to raise a defense called qualified immunity, which protects officials from some lawsuits. Another finding in this review explains it. There would be no matching liability for an agency policy or custom. The bill also says the new right does not let a federal employee sue "their Federal employer or the Federal Government". That fits this reading. Limiting liability to individuals is a design choice with arguments on both sides. One side points to the cost to the Treasury. The other points to the deterrent value of holding the agency itself liable. The text does not say which was intended.
findings.use: An agency that adopted a data program without warrants could be dismissed from a suit because it is not a "person". The plaintiff would be left to pursue the officers who carried out the program.

s.l: Return Mail, Inc. v. United States Postal Service (2019)

findings.pat: Stricter exception made redundant by a looser one

a.q: that is clearly accessible to the general public without special access or tools

findings.title: One exception covers public data only without special tools. Another exception for that data has no such limit.
findings.plain: The bill has two exceptions for public information. One covers public sources only when they can be reached "without special access or tools". The other allows the "collection or analysis" of publicly available information and puts no limit on tools. Either one is enough, so the limit on tools may do little.
findings.tech: One exception allows collection from public sources reached "without special access or tools". Another allows "collection or analysis of information that is lawfully published or voluntarily made available" to the public. That second exception limits only "circumvention of privacy settings, encryption, or other access controls", which means getting around them. It does not limit the tools used. Each exception in the bill's list stands on its own. So information that fits the second one could be collected and analyzed with automated software that gathers or monitors posts. The first exception would not allow that, but the second would. A court could instead read the more specific first exception to control, which is why confidence is medium. A later part of the bill narrows the exceptions for data gathered in certain places. Those places are public places, public roads and businesses open to the public. It does not narrow them for online posts. Another finding in this review covers who must have made the information public. This finding covers how it may be gathered.
findings.use: An agency could run social media monitoring software on public posts about a named person. It could rely on the second exception, which has no limit on tools.

findings.pat: Borrowed constitutional term carries flexible meaning

a.q: upon probable cause

findings.title: The bill asks for a warrant "upon probable cause" without saying of what. Courts could use the looser inspection standard.
findings.plain: The bill copies the Constitution's words and requires a warrant "upon probable cause". It does not say the cause must be a belief that a crime happened. The Supreme Court has read the same words to allow inspection warrants. Those warrants can rest on general program standards, not suspicion about one place. So the new warrant rule could be weaker or stronger depending on the kind of search.
findings.tech: The bill requires "a warrant issued by a neutral and detached magistrate upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation". Those words track the Constitution's warrant text. They do not tie probable cause to a crime. The Court read the same words for building inspections. The Court held "probable cause" to inspect exists if "reasonable legislative or administrative standards for conducting an area inspection are satisfied". This holds for a particular dwelling. Those standards "will not necessarily depend upon specific knowledge of the condition of the particular dwelling." The case is Camara v. Municipal Court (1967). The bill's definition of a search can reach rule-enforcement and civil inquiries. Another finding and a language question in this review cover those inquiries. So a court could use the same flexible standard for them. Or a court could require proof of a crime, which most rule-enforcement programs cannot meet. The text does not choose.
findings.use: An agency asks for a warrant to inspect records and cites Camara. A company argues the bill needs probable cause that the company broke a rule.

a.q: or other interactions with law enforcement

findings.title: Police may check an ID without a warrant in any contact. The bill does not say what checking includes.
findings.plain: Police may check a government photo ID without a warrant. This applies in a traffic stop, in travel, or in "other interactions with law enforcement". The bill does not say which contacts count. It does not say whether the contact must itself be lawful. It does not say what "verification" includes. Today a check at a traffic stop often includes looking up the driver for unpaid warrants. So "verification" could be read to include database searches.
findings.tech: The bill exempts "The verification of government-issued primary photo identification documents". This applies during a vehicle stop, travel, or "other interactions with law enforcement". The words "other interactions" are not limited to stops backed by reasonable suspicion. "Verification" is not defined. In traffic stops, the Court has said the officer's task includes "ordinary inquiries incident to [the traffic] stop". These often include "checking the driver's license," "determining whether there are outstanding warrants against the driver," and checking registration and insurance. The case is Rodriguez v. United States (2015). A court could read "verification" that way. Then it would cover checks of the person against warrant, immigration or other databases. The bill bars reading it to "authorize surveillance that would otherwise be unlawful". But such checks are lawful today. So that bar does not limit them. A database check might itself be a search. The bill leaves that open. Its definition of a search covers the "acquisition and analysis" of data. How that fits this exception is not settled.
findings.use: An officer in a casual street encounter asks for ID and runs it through several databases. The officer relies on this one exception for the whole sequence.

a.q: behavioral signals data

findings.title: The bill uses terms such as "behavioral signals data". It never says what they mean.
findings.plain: The bill's definition of a search lists items like "personal device activity" and "behavioral signals data". Its warrant rule names "data brokers" and "metadata". None of these terms is defined. Courts would give them their ordinary meaning. For newer technical terms, that meaning may be unsettled.
findings.tech: The bill defines only "search" and "plain-view searches". Other terms set how far the warrant rule reaches, and none is defined. They are "metadata" and "data brokers" in the rule on third parties. They are "agents" in the definition of a search. They are "personal device activity" and "behavioral signals data" in the list of things searched. They are "enhanced surveillance technology or systematic monitoring" in the plain-view definition, which decides when watching stops being a plain-view search. Another finding in this review covers "the government" and "a government entity". The part of the criminal code that holds the bill has no general definitions section to supply meanings. Undefined terms like these are common in federal laws. So the effect depends on how courts read each term in a real dispute.
findings.use: A party says app-use data is not "behavioral signals data". It says the same about "personal device activity". It also says location guesses fall outside the listed types.

findings.pat: Coverage of private partners left to case law
findings.title: The bill does not say if contractors, data brokers or task force partners of federal agencies can be sued.
findings.plain: The right to sue reaches anyone who acts "under color of" federal law, which means with the backing of government power. Under the main civil rights law, private parties who act jointly with officials can count. The bill does not say whether contractors, companies that supply data, or state and local officers on federal task forces are covered. So courts would decide case by case.
findings.tech: The bill makes "Every person, including a Federal employee" liable if they deprive someone of Fourth Amendment rights. It covers acts "under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage, of the United States", meaning with government backing. It names no kind of private actor. The matching state law says "Private persons, jointly engaged with state official in the challenged action are acting "under color" of law". The case is Dennis v. Sparks (1980). A court could apply the same joint-action test here. That would reach some contractors and data suppliers and not others. The text does not say which law applies to state or local officers on a federal task force. It could be federal law, state law, or both. This review did not establish the answer from a primary source.
findings.use: A plaintiff sues the contractor that ran a warrantless data pull for an agency. The contractor argues it acted on its own and not jointly with federal officials.

findings.pat: Narrow defined term beside a broad operative term

a.q: other than the President or the Vice President

findings.title: The bill leaves the President and Vice President out of "Federal employee". It also leaves out legislative and judicial staff.
findings.plain: The bill defines "Federal employee" as executive branch staff other than the President and Vice President. That leaves out, for example, police who work for Congress or the courts. The right to sue applies to "every person", so these officials may still be covered. But the bill says outright that the President and Vice President are excluded. A court could read that as a sign they were meant to be outside the law.
findings.tech: The bill defines "Federal employee" as an individual "other than the President or the Vice President". That person "occupies a position in any agency or instrumentality of the executive branch (including any independent agency)." The main text reaches "Every person, including a Federal employee". So the definition shapes the example phrase and the rule on suits by employees. It does not limit who can be sued. Officers of Congress and the courts are outside the definition. They can still act under color of federal law, which means with federal government backing. For the President, the exclusion adds little in damages cases. The Court has held that a President "is entitled to absolute immunity from damages liability" for official acts. The case is Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982). That holding did not cover the Vice President. A court could read the express exclusion to mean Congress did not want the new right to sue to reach either office.
findings.use: A Vice President's office is sued under the new right to sue. It argues that the definition's exclusion shows Congress meant to exempt the office.

a.q: for conduct that is within the scope of the employment relationship

findings.title: The bill limits suits by federal workers. It does not say if the limit covers suits against supervisors over monitoring.
findings.plain: The bill does not let a federal employee sue "their Federal employer or the Federal Government". This covers conduct within the job. It does not say whether "employer" includes a supervisor. It does not say whose conduct must be within that job. Read broadly, the rule could limit suits over monitoring of federal workers' devices or personal accounts.
findings.tech: The bill says nothing in it authorizes "a Federal employee to bring a suit against their Federal employer or the Federal Government". This is for conduct "that is within the scope of the employment relationship." Suits against agencies and the United States are already barred. Another finding in this review says why. So this rule adds the most if "Federal employer" includes supervisors sued as people. The phrase "within the scope of the employment relationship" is also undefined. It could mean the worker's conduct, the supervisor's conduct, or the monitoring program. The text does not say how far the rule reaches. Examples are insider-threat programs, device searches and monitoring of personal accounts. A court would have to decide.
findings.use: A supervisor is sued over a search of an employee's phone. The supervisor says the rule covers a "Federal employer" like the supervisor.

findings.pat: Two-way fee shifting copied from section 1988

a.q: may allow the prevailing party, other than the United States

findings.title: The bill lets a winning officer who was sued, not only a winning plaintiff, ask for attorney's fees.
findings.plain: The fee rule applies to "the prevailing party, other than the United States". So an officer who wins could ask the person who sued to pay the officer's lawyers. Under the civil rights law with the same wording, courts give fees to winning defendants only when the suit was frivolous. The bill does not say that.
findings.tech: The bill allows fees to "the prevailing party, other than the United States". That wording tracks the federal civil rights law on attorney's fees. Under that law, a winning defendant gets fees only "upon a finding that the plaintiff's action was frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation." The case is Fox v. Vice (2011). A court would likely apply the same standard to matching text. But the bill does not state it, so the standard depends on the court choosing to borrow it. Another finding in this review covers the fee rule's reference to "this Act".
findings.use: An officer wins because of qualified immunity, a shield for officials against some suits. The officer asks for fees and says the claim had no basis.

bigger.issue: Protection from government searches in the digital age
bigger.lead: Suppose every part of the surveillance bill worked as intended. It would put a warrant rule on how the government gets data. A warrant is permission from a judge. For the reasons below, the bill would still not by itself end searches done without warrants.

map.part: Government access to personal data held by companies
map.note: The bill's main rule says the government needs a warrant to get data that companies hold. A warrant is permission from a judge.

map.part: Government purchases of personal data from data brokers
map.note: Buying data from brokers counts as "access" under the bill, meaning getting the data. But the bill never mentions buying or contractors.

map.part: Collection and sale of personal data by private companies
map.note: The bill does not require anything of companies that collect or sell personal data. The data stays open to other buyers, including foreign ones.

map.part: Foreign intelligence spying that collects Americans' data
map.note: Separate laws and the President's own power govern this spying. The bill never mentions them.

map.part: Older court orders, subpoenas and FBI demand letters that need less than a warrant
map.note: The bill does not say it overrides these older powers. It also does not change the laws that create them.

map.part: State and local surveillance
map.note: The bill does not define the words "the government". So it is unclear if the bill covers state and local agencies.

map.part: Government-run face scanning and license plate readers
map.note: The bill deals with face scans and plate readers only through a limit on its exceptions. How far that limit reaches is unclear.

map.part: Personal data that agencies already hold
map.note: The bill has no rule on data agencies already hold. It does not say if they may keep, delete or search it.

map.part: What happens when the warrant rule is broken
map.note: People could sue only over breaking the Constitution. Evidence would not be kept out of court. The bill says nothing about officials' immunity, meaning protection from paying damages.

map.part: Public reporting and oversight of government searches
map.note: The bill requires no reports, no audits and no notice to people who were searched.

map.part: Searches and data collection outside the United States
map.note: The bill does not say it applies abroad. One court ruling says federal laws "will be construed to have only domestic application" unless Congress clearly says otherwise. The ruling is RJR Nabisco Inc v European Community (2016). So the new warrant rule would presumably not reach searches done in other countries. This presumption applies to every federal law that is silent on the point.

s.l: RJR Nabisco, Inc. v. European Community (2016)

map.part: Court and agency capacity for more warrant applications
map.note: The bill would require warrants for kinds of access that now use subpoenas, orders or no process. It gives no money, guidance, transition time or study of the added work for courts and agencies.

others.l: Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act (passed the House in April 2024)
others.n: Aimed specifically at law enforcement and intelligence purchases from data brokers.
A bipartisan Senate measure that works through the foreign intelligence statutes directly.
The first state to bar its agencies from buying data they would otherwise need a warrant to obtain.

stake.want: Privacy and civil liberties advocates want a warrant rule with no gaps. They also want the government to stop buying people's data from data brokers.
Federal crime investigators want to get records fast, and lawfully, in cases of fraud, trafficking and missing people. Critics of the bill say warrant rules slow these cases down.
Intelligence and counterterrorism officials work on spying and on stopping terror attacks. They want to keep their foreign spy powers as they are.
State and local police want to keep using license plate readers and shared databases. They also want a clear answer on whether the warrant rule binds them.

stake.role: Data brokers and ad tech companies
stake.want: Data brokers and ad tech companies want to keep selling personal data. The government would be one customer among many.
Companies that hold customer data want a clear rule on when they must hand data to the government. They also do not want to be blamed for following it.
People who are watched the most want the same protection no matter which agency gets their data. News reports show local camera data reaching immigration agents.
Crime victims and those who speak up for them want investigations to move fast when someone is in danger.

stake.role: Sponsors of the Surveillance Accountability Act
stake.want: The bill's sponsors want a warrant for every government search. They describe the bill as covering federal and local agencies.

stake.role: Members of Congress who want to renew current surveillance law first
stake.want: Some members of Congress want current surveillance powers renewed first. They would leave wider changes for later.

stake.role: Civil rights lawyers who would sue under the bill
stake.want: Civil rights lawyers who would sue under the bill want a right to sue that courts will not throw out early.

stake.role: Government lawyers who would defend those lawsuits
stake.want: Government lawyers who would defend cases under the bill want each of its demands read as narrowly as they can.

stake.role: A judge who follows a law's exact words
stake.want: A judge who follows a law's exact words applies them as written. This judge will not fill in what Congress left out.

stake.role: A judge who looks to a law's purpose
stake.want: A judge who looks to a law's purpose settles doubts in favor of what the law was trying to do.
A legislative drafter writes bills. A drafter wants every key word defined and every reference checked. A drafter also wants every link to current law spelled out.

conflicts.claim: Under the surveillance bill, an agency that wants your data would decide for itself if it needs a warrant.
conflicts.detail: Each agency would decide if its own data collection counts as a search under the bill. It would also decide if one of the bill's exceptions applies. A judge would review a search only when the agency decided it needed a warrant and asked for one. The bill requires no report or check when the agency decides it does not.

conflicts.who: Each agency that does a search
conflicts.claim: The agency doing a search would decide if an emergency or a person's consent lets it skip the warrant.
conflicts.detail: Emergencies and consent are two of the bill's exceptions to the warrant rule. The agency that gains from an exception would decide if it applies. The bill requires no review after an agency relies on one.

plain.conf_note: No conflicts involving named people have been looked into for this bill. It is not law, and it gives no job to a named official.
